section.heading: 3.3. Derivatives of Trigonometric Functions
section.paragraph: Before starting this section, you might need to review the trigonometric functions. In particular, it is important to remember that when we talk about the function $$f$$ defined for all real numbers $$x$$ by
$$f(x) = \sin x$$

it is understood that $$\sin x$$ means the sine of the angle whose radian measure is $$x$$ . A similar convention holds for the other trigonometric functions $$\cos$$ , $$\tan$$ , $$\csc$$ , $$\sec$$ , and $$\cot$$ . Recall from Section 2.5 that all of the trigonometric functions are continuous at every number in their domains.
A review of the trigonometric functions is given in Appendix D.
section.heading: Derivatives of the Trigonometric Functions
section.paragraph: If we sketch the graph of the function $$f(x) = \sin x$$ and use the interpretation of $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ as the slope of the tangent to the sine curve in order to sketch the graph of $$f^{\prime}$$ (see Exercise 2.8.16), then it looks as if the graph of $$f^{\prime}$$ may be the same as the cosine curve (see Figure 1).

image.alt: Details Two graphs display a curve on the x y coordinate plane one below the other such that their tick marks are aligned. The origin of the first and the second graphs are vertically aligned. In both the graphs, the x axis is displayed from negative 2 pi to 2 pi in increments of pi/2 units. In both the graphs, the curve increases and decreases with alternating high and low points at regular intervals, reaching the same y-coordinate for each maximum and minimum. The curve labeled y = f(x) = sin(x) enters the third quadrant, goes up and to the right by crossing the x axis at (negative 2 pi, 0), reaches a high point at (negative 3 pi/2, 1), goes down and to the right, crosses the x axis at (negative pi, 0), falls below the x axis, reaches a low point at (negative pi/2, negative 1), then goes up and to the right through the origin until it reaches a high point at (pi/2, 1). It then goes down and to the right through (pi, 0), reaches a minimum at (3 pi/2, negative 1), then goes up and to the right through (2 pi, 0), and continues in this fashion as it proceeds to the right. The horizontal tangents which are lying above the curve touch the sine curve exactly once at its high points. The horizontal tangents which are lying below the curve touch the sine curve exactly once at its low points. The tangents with a negative slope almost appear to lie along the sine curve and touch it exactly once at (negative pi, 0) and (pi, 0). A tangent with a positive slope almost appears to lie along the curve while rising through the origin and touches it exactly once at the origin. In the second graph, the curve y = f prime (x) enters the second quadrant, rises to a high point (negative 2 pi, 1), goes down and to the right, crosses the x axis at (negative 3 pi/2, 0), goes down and to the right, reaches a low point at (negative pi, negative 1), goes up and to the right by crossing the x axis again at (negative pi/2, 0), and reaches a high point at (0, 1). It then goes down and to the right by crossing the x axis at (pi/2, 0), reaches a low point at (pi, negative 1), again goes up and to the right, crossing the x axis at (3 pi/2, 0), then reaches a high point again at (2 pi, 1), and continues in this fashion as it proceeds to the right. The high and low points of the sine curve are vertically aligned with the x-intercepts of y = f prime (x). Similarly, the x-intercepts of the sine curve are vertically aligned with the high and low points of y = f prime (x).

section.paragraph: Two of these four limits are easy to evaluate. Because we regard $$x$$ as a constant when computing a limit as $$\left. h\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ , we have
$$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\sin x = \sin x$$
and
$$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\cos x = \cos x$$
Later in this section we will prove that
$$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sin h}{h} = 1$$
and
$$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\cos h - 1}{h} = 0$$
Putting these limits into (1), we get

$$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\sin x \cdot \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\cos h - 1}{h} + \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\cos x \cdot \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sin h}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\left( {\sin x} \right) \cdot 0 + \left( {\cos x} \right) \cdot 1 = \cos x}} \end{array}$$
So we have proved the formula for the derivative of the sine function:
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\sin x} \right) = \cos x$$

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Differentiate $$y = x^{2}\sin x$$ .
Solution Using the Product Rule and Formula 2, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{dy}{\mathit{dx}} = {x^{2}\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{({\sin x})} + \sin x\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{(x^{2})}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{dy}{\mathit{dx}}} = {x^{2}\cos x + 2x\sin x}} \end{array}$$
Figure 2 shows the graphs of the function of Example 1 and its derivative. Notice that $$y^{\prime} = 0$$ whenever $$y$$ has a horizontal tangent.

section.paragraph: Using the same methods as in the proof of Formula 2, one can prove (see Exercise 26) that
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\cos x} \right) = - \sin x$$
The tangent function can also be differentiated by using the definition of a derivative, but it is easier to use the Quotient Rule together with Formulas 2 and 3:

$$\begin{array}{lc} {{\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\tan x} \right)} = {\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( \frac{\sin x}{\cos x} \right)}} & \\ {\phantom{\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\tan x} \right)} = \frac{\cos x\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\sin x} \right) - \sin x\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\cos x} \right)}{\cos^{2}x}} & \\ {\phantom{\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\tan x} \right)} = \frac{\cos x \cdot \cos x - \sin x\left( {- \sin x} \right)}{\cos^{2}x}} & \\ {\phantom{\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\tan x} \right)} = \frac{\cos^{2}x + \sin^{2}x}{\cos^{2}x}} & { \left( \cos^{2}x + \sin^{2}x = 1 \right)} \\ {\phantom{\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\tan x} \right)} = {\frac{1}{\cos^{2}x} = \sec^{2}x}} & \end{array}$$
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\tan x} \right) = \sec^{2}x$$

The derivatives of the remaining trigonometric functions, $$\csc$$ , $$\sec$$ , and $$\cot$$ , can also be found easily using the Quotient Rule (see Exercises 23, 24, and 25). We collect all the differentiation formulas for trigonometric functions in the following table. Remember that they are valid only when $$x$$ is measured in radians.

note.title: Derivatives of Trigonometric Functions
note.heading: Derivatives of Trigonometric Functions
note.paragraph: $$\begin{array}{ll} {\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\sin x} \right) = \cos x} & { \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\csc x} \right) = - \csc x\cot x} \\ {\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\cos x} \right) = - \sin x} & { \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\sec x} \right) = \sec x\tan x} \\ {\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\tan x} \right) = \sec^{2}x} & { \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\cot x} \right) = - \csc^{2}x} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: When you memorize this table, it is helpful to notice that the minus signs go with the derivatives of the “cofunctions,” that is, cosine, cosecant, and cotangent.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Differentiate $$f(x) = \frac{\sec x}{1 + \tan x}$$ . For what values of $$x$$ does the graph of $$f$$ have a horizontal tangent?
Solution The Quotient Rule gives

$$\begin{array}{lc} {{f^{\prime}(x)} = \frac{\left( {1 + \tan x} \right)\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\sec x} \right) - \sec x\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {1 + \tan x} \right)}{\left( {1 + \tan x} \right)^{2}}} & \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = \frac{\left( {1 + \tan x} \right)\sec x\tan x - \sec x \cdot \sec^{2}x}{\left( {1 + \tan x} \right)^{2}}} & \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = \frac{\sec x\left( {\tan x + \tan^{2}x - \sec^{2}x} \right)}{\left( {1 + \tan x} \right)^{2}}} & \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = \frac{\sec x\left( {\tan x - 1} \right)}{\left( {1 + \tan x} \right)^{2}}} & { \left( \sec^{2}x = \tan^{2}x + 1 \right)} \end{array}$$
Because $$\sec x$$ is never $$0$$ , we see that $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ when $$\tan x = 1$$ , and this occurs when $$x = \pi \slash 4 + n\pi$$ , where $$n$$ is an integer (see Figure 3).

section.paragraph: Trigonometric functions are often used in modeling real-world phenomena. In particular, vibrations, waves, elastic motions, and other quantities that vary in a periodic manner can be described using trigonometric functions. In the following example we discuss an instance of simple harmonic motion.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: An object fastened to the end of a vertical spring is stretched $$4$$ cm beyond its rest position and released at time $$t = 0$$ . (See Figure 4 and note that the downward direction is positive.) Its position at time $$t$$ is
$$s = f(t) = 4\cos t$$
Find the velocity and acceleration at time $$t$$ and use them to analyze the motion of the object.

image.alt: Details An illustration shows a spring suspended vertically, with a hook at each end. The top hook is latched to another hook from horizontal support on top. An object is attached to the bottom hook and the spring is then stretched downward. To its right, a vertical number line labeled s is displayed from negative 4 to beyond 4 in increments of 4 units, in the order from top to bottom such that the number 4 is aligned with the attached object.

example.paragraph: Solution The velocity and acceleration are

$$\begin{array}{lll} \upsilon & = & {\frac{ds}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}\left( {4\cos t} \right) = 4\frac{d}{dt}\left( {\cos t} \right) = - 4\sin t} \\ a & = & {\frac{\mathit{dv}}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}\left( {- 4\sin t} \right) = - 4\frac{d}{dt}\left( {\sin t} \right) = - 4\cos t} \end{array}$$

The object oscillates from the lowest point $$\left( {s = 4{cm}} \right)$$ to the highest point $$\left( {s = - 4{cm}} \right)$$ . The period of the oscillation is $$2\pi$$ , the period of $$\cos t$$ .

The speed is $$|\upsilon| = 4\left| {\sin t} \right|$$ , which is greatest when $$\left| {\sin t} \right| = 1$$ , that is, when $$\cos t = 0$$ . So the object moves fastest as it passes through its equilibrium position $$\left( {s = 0} \right)$$ . Its speed is $$0$$ when $$\sin t = 0$$ , that is, at the highest and lowest points.
The acceleration $$a = - 4\cos t = 0$$ when $$s = 0$$ . It has greatest magnitude at the highest and lowest points. See the graphs in Figure 5.

section.paragraph: The first special limit we considered concerned the sine function. The following special limit involves cosine.
$$\lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow 0}\frac{\cos\theta - 1}{\theta} = 0$$

note.title: Proof
note.heading: Proof
note.paragraph: We multiply numerator and denominator by $$\cos\theta + 1$$ in order to put the function in a form in which we can use limits that we know.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Find $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sin 7x}{4x}$$ .
Solution In order to apply Equation 5, we first rewrite the function by multiplying and dividing by $$7$$ :
$$\frac{\sin 7x}{4x} = \frac{7}{4}\left( \frac{\sin 7x}{7x} \right)$$
If we let $$\theta = 7x$$ , then $$\left. \theta\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ , so by Equation 5 we have

$$\begin{array}{lll} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sin 7x}{4x}} & = & {\frac{7}{4}\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\left( \frac{\sin 7x}{7x} \right)} \\ \phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} & = & {\frac{7}{4}\lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta} = \frac{7}{4} \cdot 1 = \frac{7}{4}} \end{array}$$
Note that $$\sin 7x \neq 7\sin x$$ .

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: Find $$\lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow 0}\frac{\cos\theta - 1}{\sin\theta}$$ .
Solution In order to use Equations 5 and 6 we divide numerator and denominator by $$\theta$$ :

$$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow 0}\frac{\cos\theta - 1}{\sin\theta} = \lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow 0}\frac{\frac{\cos\theta - 1}{\theta}}{\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow 0}\frac{\cos\theta - 1}{\sin\theta}} = \frac{\lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow 0}\frac{\cos\theta - 1}{\theta}}{\lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta}} = \frac{0}{1} = 0} \end{array}$$
